newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech government faces hot summer after reprieve.
newsitem.headline: Czech government faces hot summer after reprieve.

text.p: Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus faces a summer of discontent despite narrowly winning a parliamentary confidence vote, as a new survey on Wednesday showed Czechs' faith in his centre-right cabinet ebbing away.

Analysts said it could only get tougher for post-Communist Europe's most enduring ruling coalition as it sought to enact sharp budget cuts and wage freezes to solve problems which Klaus himself says grew, in part, from poor policy decisions.

Klaus avoided being ousted late on Tuesday, cutting a last-minute deal with an independent deputy to squeak home in a confidence vote for his three-party cabinet and its package of tough austerity measures by 101-99 in the lower house.
"Despite the confidence vote, the government will remain unstable," independent political analyst Jiri Pehe said.
"It faces challenges much bigger than those it faced when it still enjoyed public support and when the coalition was relatively united."

Klaus, widely credited as chief architect of the country's rapid post-Communist transformation but pilloried for recent economic woes, leads a coalition which controls only half of the powerful lower house.

The coalition has been rocked by recent infighting between the two rightwing parties and the centrist Christian Democrats, and is not assured of getting the cross-over votes it needs to enact potentially unpopular legislation.
A new opinion poll released on Wednesday showed public support for the coalition had fallen to its lowest level yet.

The survey, taken by the state Institute for Public Opinion Research from May 30 to June 3, showed combined support for the three parties in the government at 38.5 percent, down from 42.5 in an early May poll.
But Klaus's rightwing Civic Democratic Party edged up two percentage points from its worst showing ever in the early-May poll, to 20 percent.
The new survey, however, came soon after the coalition package of emergency economic measures was announced on May 28.

The austerity programme, which was accompanied by the cabinet's acknowledgement of policy mistakes, followed an economic downturn and a speculative attack on the crown which forced the central bank to float the currency.

The junior coalition parties, the pro-business Civic Democratic Alliance and the centrist Christian Democrats saw their support in the poll fall to seven and 11.5 percent respectively from 10 and 14.5 percent a month ago.
With battles certain over 1997 budget cuts, a leader of the largest opposition party, the Social Democrats, sounded an ominous note:
"I have a feeling that this summer won't be very peaceful," Stanislav Gross, the head of the Social Democrats parliamentary conference told Czech Radio on Tuesday.
"The discussion on the 1998 budget will begin during these months and I expect that it will not be especially quiet."
The Social Democrats led all parties in the IVVM survey, rising to 28 percent from 25 percent, its highest level ever.
The combined popularity of the opposition parties, including the far-left Communists and ultra-right Republicans, rose to 40 percent from 34 percent.

The Social Democrats have made soundings about forming a possible coalition with the Christian Democrats should the current government fall, but they have ruled out any coalition with the Republicans and the Communists.
The next general elections are scheduled for June 2000, but Social Democrat leaders have said that they expect early elections to be needed by the autumn of next year.
